conceptPrimer.heading: Lensmaker's Formula: Where Focus Comes From
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A thin lens of glass index $n_g$ in a surrounding medium $n_m$ has $\frac{1}{f} = \left(\frac{n_g}{n_m} - 1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$. Focus exists only when the refractive-index CONTRAST is non-zero — in matched media a lens goes blind ($f \to \infty$). For an equiconvex lens in air ($R_1 = +R$, $R_2 = -R$), $\frac{1}{f} = \left(n_g - 1\right)\frac{2}{R}$. Micro-check: equiconvex with $R = 20\ \text{cm}$, $n_g = 1.5$ in air: $\frac{1}{f} = 0.5 \times \tfrac{2}{20} = \tfrac{1}{20}$, so $f = +20\ \text{cm}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Immersion: Same Lens, New Focus
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: In a denser surrounding medium the contrast $\frac{n_g}{n_m} - 1$ shrinks, so $|f|$ GROWS: a lens weakens in water. The standard clean pair is $n_g = 1.5$ in water ($n_m = \tfrac{4}{3}$): the contrast drops from $\tfrac{1}{2}$ to $\tfrac{1}{8}$ — exactly $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of the power, so focal length becomes $4f_{\text{air}}$. If $n_m > n_g$ the lens even flips behaviour. Micro-check: the $R = 20\ \text{cm}$ equiconvex above gains $f = 4 \times 20 = 80\ \text{cm}$ underwater.

conceptPrimer.heading: Thin-Lens Equation and Its Magnification
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: The lens equation carries a MINUS: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$, with Cartesian signs ($u < 0$ for real objects). Magnification is $m = +\frac{v}{u}$ — no minus sign, unlike mirrors. Converging lenses give real inverted images for objects beyond $f$, virtual upright magnified ones inside $f$ (the magnifier regime); a diverging lens always shrinks virtually. Micro-check: $f = +10\ \text{cm}$, $u = -15\ \text{cm}$: $\frac{1}{v} = \tfrac{1}{10} - \tfrac{1}{15} = \tfrac{1}{30} \Rightarrow v = +30\ \text{cm}$, real, and $m = +\tfrac{30}{-15} = -2$ — inverted, doubled.

conceptPrimer.heading: Cutting Lenses: Transverse vs Horizontal
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Cutting an equiconvex lens of focal length $f$ TRANSVERSELY (perpendicular to the axis, into two plano-convex halves) turns each half into $f' = 2f$ — power halves, aperture halves. Cutting HORIZONTALLY along the principal axis only splits the aperture: each piece still has focal length $f$. Either way a full image still forms — intensity, not existence, is what aperture controls. Micro-check: an $f = 10\ \text{cm}$ equiconvex cut transversely yields two $f = 20\ \text{cm}$ plano-convex lenses.

conceptPrimer.heading: Optical Power, Combinations and Silvered Lenses
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Power $P = \frac{1}{f\ (\text{metres})} = \frac{100}{f\ (\text{cm})}$ dioptres — the unit trap lives here ($f = 20\ \text{cm} \Rightarrow P = +5\ \text{D}$, never $+0.05$). Coaxial thin lenses combine as $P_{\text{eq}} = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1P_2$; in contact ($d = 0$) powers simply add, and a real-plus-virtual pair can cancel. A lens silvered on one face acts as a mirror: $\frac{1}{F} = \frac{2}{f_{\text{lens}}} + \frac{1}{f_{\text{mirror}}}$. Micro-check: $P_1 = +4\ \text{D}$ touching $P_2 = -2\ \text{D}$ gives $P_{\text{eq}} = +2\ \text{D}$, i.e. $f = +50\ \text{cm}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: The $D \ge 4f$ Screen Rule and Displacement Method
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A converging lens can throw a real image on a screen only when object and screen are separated by $D \ge 4f$; at exactly $D = 4f$ the lens sits at the midpoint with a single (same-size) image. For $D > 4f$ there are TWO positions giving sharp images, and the displacement method reads $f = \frac{D^2 - d^2}{4D}$ from the separation $d$ of those positions. Micro-check: $f = 25\ \text{cm}$ demands at least $4 \times 25 = 100\ \text{cm} = 1\ \text{m}$ between object and screen.

Parallel rays meet at the focus; $f > 0$ in Cartesian convention.
Parallel rays spread as if from the focus; $f < 0$.
The interior point through which rays pass undeviated and undisplaced.
The effective diameter gathering light; sets image brightness, not completeness.
Unit of lens power: inverse focal length in metres; converging positive, diverging negative.
The line through both centres of curvature and the optical centre.
Formed by actual ray convergence on the far side; projectable and inverted.
Seen through the lens on the object side; upright, not projectable.

memoryHooks: Lensmaker's lesson: no index contrast, no focus — matched media blind the lens.
Water weakens lenses: $1.5$ glass in $4/3$ water makes $f$ four times longer.
Lens equation carries the MINUS; mirror equation the PLUS.
Lens magnification is $+v/u$ — one sign fewer than the mirror.
Transverse cut doubles $f$; horizontal cut only slices aperture.
Contact powers add; separated powers lose $dP_1P_2$.
A blocked half-aperture still forms a full image — just dimmer.
Screen experiments need $D \ge 4f$; exactly $4f$ gives one same-size image.
Inside the focus, a convex lens turns magnifier.
commonMistakes: Feeding centimetres into $P = 1/f$ — dioptres demand metres.
Writing the lens equation with the mirror's plus sign.
Attaching the mirror's minus sign to lens magnification ($m = +v/u$).
Saying a water-immersed lens keeps $f$ — that is true only for mirrors.
Claiming a transverse cut leaves $f$ unchanged (each plano-convex half is $2f$).
Using $P_{\text{eq}} = P_1 + P_2$ when a separation $d$ is given.
Expecting a half-painted lens to form a half image.
Setting up a screen experiment at $D < 4f$ and hunting for a sharp image that cannot exist.
examChecklist: Apply the lensmaker formula with $R_1 > 0$, $R_2 < 0$ for convex surfaces.
Immersion numerics: recompute the contrast $\frac{n_g}{n_m} - 1$ first.
Write Cartesian signs for $u$, $v$, $f$ before solving $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$.
Report images with position + nature + size (all three).
Convert $f$ to metres before any dioptre arithmetic.
Coaxial combinations: powers add only at $d = 0$; otherwise subtract $dP_1P_2$.
Cut-lens questions: identify transverse vs horizontal before applying the rule.
Screen problems: check $D \ge 4f$ first, then the displacement formula if needed.
Half-aperture answers: complete image, reduced intensity — always.
Magnifier regime: confirm $u < f$ before promising upright magnification.
